analysis_pairs.text_N1:
There’s another layer underneath all this, one that’s harder to see but might be the most important of all: **what you think you owe the audience.**

When you step in front of people, you probably carry an invisible expectation: *I must be polished, articulate, and never show cracks.* That expectation comes from a culture that worships “effortless perfection.” We see TED talks with speakers who seem flawless, and we forget that behind the scenes there were dozens of rehearsals, edits, and probably a few wiped-out moments. We compare our raw, unedited selves to someone else’s highlight reel. And then we freeze—not because we’re inadequate, but because we’re trying to meet an impossible standard.

But what if the audience doesn’t actually need perfection from you? What if they need **presence** instead? Presence is not the absence of mistakes. Presence is the quality of being fully there, connected to your material and to the people in the room. A speaker who is present can pause, lose their thread, even admit confusion, and still hold the room. Because the audience senses that they’re with a real person, not a performance. And real people are interesting. Real people are trustworthy. Real people are relatable.

So the freeze may have been a signal that you were stuck in performance mode—trying to get it right, trying to appear a certain way—and your system short-circuited under the pressure. The way out is not to try harder to perform. The way out is to shift your goal from *performing well* to *being present and useful.* Ask yourself before your next talk: “What do I want to give these people?” instead of “What will they think of me?” That single shift can lower the stakes dramatically.

**Shame resilience** is another piece. Brené Brown, who studies shame, says shame gets its power from secrecy, silence, and judgment. The antidote is to recognize shame, name it, and tell your story to someone who has earned the right to hear it. You’ve already started doing that here—by telling me, a stranger, what happened. That act of speaking it out loud, even anonymously, begins to loosen shame’s grip. The next step is to tell one trusted person in your real life. Watch their face. Notice their lack of horror. Notice their empathy. Shame can’t survive empathy. It shrivels in the light.

And here’s something surprising: **confidence is not built by avoiding moments of vulnerability. It’s built by surviving them.** Think of any skill you’ve ever developed—riding a bike, learning a language, cooking a new dish. You didn’t get better by never falling. You got better by falling, getting back up, and trying again. Each time you survived a wobble, you learned: *I can handle this.* The same is true for public speaking. This freeze, as painful as it is, is one of those falls. It’s proof that you were in the arena, trying something that matters to you. And you survived it. You’re still here, still breathing, still capable of thinking about it with clarity. That survival is more valuable than a flawless speech, because it builds self-trust.

**Self-trust** is the quiet knowledge that you will be there for yourself, no matter what. When you make a mistake and respond with self-criticism, you break that trust. You teach yourself that you are a harsh judge, not an ally. But when you respond with compassion—“Okay, that was rough, and I’m not going to beat myself up for it”—you keep that trust intact. You become your own safe place to land. And that changes everything about how you approach pressure, because you’re no longer terrified of your own inner voice.

There’s also a difference between **rumination and reflection.** Rumination is the repetitive, self-punishing replay of the event. It asks, “Why did I do that? What’s wrong with me?” and it never arrives at an answer. It just keeps you stuck in the feeling. Reflection, on the other hand, asks, “What happened? What can I learn? What would I do differently next time?” and then moves on. You can’t control which one shows up, but you can decide which one you feed. When you catch yourself ruminating, gently redirect to reflection. Write down one lesson. One thing you’ll try next time. Then close the notebook. The goal isn’t to never think about it again; it’s to not let it dominate your mental space.

**Self-forgiveness** might feel like a strange concept here, but it applies. You need to forgive yourself for being human. For having a body that responds to stress in ways you can’t always control. For not being perfect. This is not about letting yourself off the hook—it’s about releasing the hook entirely. You don’t need to be punished. You need to be understood. You need to be accepted as you are, freeze and all. When you can say, “I forgive myself for freezing. I was doing the best I could under a lot of pressure,” you reclaim your power from the moment.

Finally, consider this: **the freeze might be a gift.** Not a pleasant one, but a useful one. It might be telling you something. Maybe you need to slow down. Maybe you need to prepare differently. Maybe you need to care less about what others think. Maybe you need to ask for support. Maybe you need to practice in front of smaller groups first. Maybe you need to reconnect with why you’re speaking in the first place—what you’re trying to say, who you’re trying to help. Every painful experience carries information. Don’t waste this one by just feeling bad about it. Mine it for insight.

You asked me to say more, and I’m saying this: you are not broken. You are not less than. You are not a cautionary tale. You are a person who cares deeply about doing good work, and that care sometimes overwhelms you. That’s not a flaw. That’s a sign of how much this matters to you. The next time you stand in front of people, you’ll carry this experience with you—not as a wound, but as a reminder that you’ve been there, you’ve felt the fear, and you came out the other side. That’s not something to be ashamed of. That’s something to be proud of.

So tonight, let yourself off the hook. Tomorrow, take one small step forward. And whenever the memory of the freeze comes back, say to yourself: “That was one moment. I am more than one moment. And I’m still learning.” Because that’s the truth. And the truth, spoken kindly, is exactly what you need.

Not because it was pleasant—it wasn’t—but because it might force you to finally let go of a version of yourself that was never sustainable: the version that always has it together, never stumbles, never shows cracks.

That version of you was always a fiction. And the freezing moment was simply the truth breaking through the fiction. It was your body saying, “I can’t keep this up. I need you to see me as I actually am.” That might sound terrifying, but it’s also liberating. Because when you stop trying to be perfect, you get to be real. And real is where connection happens. Real is where confidence grows. Real is where you can finally rest.

**The breaking is not the end. It’s the beginning of something more honest.**

Think of kintsugi, the Japanese art of repairing broken pottery with gold. The cracks are not hidden. They’re filled with gold, making the piece more beautiful and more valuable for having been broken. This freeze is a crack. It’s a place where you felt exposed, where you felt like you fell apart. But if you allow it, that crack can be filled with gold—with self-compassion, with wisdom, with a deeper understanding of yourself. You don’t have to pretend it didn’t happen. You can let it become part of your story, a visible seam that shows you survived. And that seam, when you share it with others, becomes a source of strength. It says: I am human. I have stumbled. And I am still here.

**The audience doesn’t need you to be a statue. They need you to be a guide—someone who has walked through the fire and can show them the way.**

Now, let’s talk about the inner critic. That voice that says, “You should be mortified. You should feel ashamed. You need to be harder on yourself so this never happens again.” That voice is not your friend, but it is trying to protect you. It believes that if it shames you enough, you’ll never make that mistake again. But shame doesn’t work that way. Shame makes you smaller. It makes you avoid taking risks. It makes you hide. It makes you more likely to freeze again, because you’re now terrified of the shame that will follow.

The way to quiet that voice is not to argue with it, but to thank it and move on. “Thank you for trying to keep me safe. I know you’re scared. But I’m going to be kind to myself now.” Say it out loud if you need to. It sounds silly, but it works. You’re not ignoring the inner critic; you’re acknowledging it and then choosing a different path. Over time, that voice gets quieter, because you stop feeding it with your attention.

**Practice self-compassion as a discipline, not a feeling.** It’s not about waiting until you feel like being kind to yourself. It’s about doing it even when you don’t feel like it. Especially when you don’t feel like it. Put your hand on your heart. Say: “This is hard. I’m doing the best I can. I’m allowed to make mistakes.” These are not empty affirmations; they are neurological interventions. They signal to your nervous system that you are safe, that you are not alone, that you are cared for. And that signal changes everything.

**Now, let’s talk about rebuilding confidence.** Confidence is not the absence of fear. It’s the belief that you can handle whatever happens, even if you’re scared. That belief is built through experience—through surviving hard things and learning that you can cope. This freeze is one of those hard things. You are surviving it right now. You’re reaching out, you’re reflecting, you’re not collapsing into permanent despair. That is resilience. That is the seed of confidence.

To rebuild, start small. Give yourself opportunities to speak in low-stakes settings. Tell a story at dinner. Ask a question in a meeting. Practice saying, “I don’t know, let me think about that,” without shame. Each small success, each moment of choosing courage over avoidance, rewires your brain. It teaches you: I can do hard things. I can be uncomfortable. I can survive.

And when you do stand up to speak again—and you will—don’t aim for perfection. Aim for connection. Look at one friendly face. Speak a little slower than feels natural. Let there be silence. If you lose your place, say, “Give me a moment,” and take a breath. That pause will feel like an eternity, but I promise you, it will be over before you know it. And the audience will not punish you for it. They will wait. Because they want you to succeed. They want to hear what you have to say.

A story about a person who cared so much that their body said “stop.” A person who felt mortified and then got up anyway. A person who learned that being human is not a weakness, but a deep, unshakable strength.

One day, you’ll tell this story to someone else who is shaking in their shoes before a presentation. You’ll tell them how you froze, how you thought your career was over, how you lay awake replaying it. And then you’ll tell them how you got through it. How you learned to be kinder to yourself. How you spoke again, and trembled, and still did it. And you’ll watch their shoulders drop, and their eyes soften, because they see that you survived. And then they’ll know they can, too.

So tonight, let the tears come if they need to. Let the cringe wash over you. And then, before you sleep, say this to yourself: “I am allowed to be human. I am allowed to need a pause. I am allowed to move on. And I will.” Because you are, and you will. Not because you’re perfect, but because you’re learning. And that is enough. More than enough. It’s everything.

It makes you more likely to freeze again, because you’re now terrified of the shame that will follow.

But I’m going to be kind to myself now.” Say it out loud if you need to. It sounds silly, but it works. They signal to your nervous system that you are safe, that you are not alone, that you are cared for. And that signal changes everything.

That belief is built through experience—through surviving hard things and learning that you can cope. This freeze is one of those hard things. You are surviving it right now. You’re reaching out, you’re reflecting, you’re not collapsing into permanent despair. That is resilience. That is the seed of confidence.

To rebuild, start small. Give yourself opportunities to speak in low-stakes settings. Tell a story at dinner. Ask a question in a meeting. Practice saying, “I don’t know, let me think about that,” without shame. Each small success, each moment of choosing courage over avoidance, rewires your brain. It teaches you: I can do hard things. I can be uncomfortable. I can survive.

And when you do stand up to speak again—and you will—don’t aim for perfection. Aim for connection. Look at one friendly face. Speak a little slower than feels natural. Let there be silence. If you lose your place, say, “Give me a moment,” and take a breath. That pause will feel like an eternity, but I promise you, it will be over before you know it. And the audience will not punish you for it. They will wait. Because they want you to succeed. They want to hear what you have to say.

**Finally, let me leave you with this thought: the most powerful thing you can do is not to erase the memory of the freeze, but to change your relationship to it.** Instead of seeing it as a failure that defines you, see it as a story you get to tell. A story about a person who cared so much that their body said “stop.” A person who felt mortified and then got up anyway. A person who learned that being human is not a weakness, but a deep, unshakable strength.

One day, you’ll tell this story to someone else who is shaking in their shoes before a presentation. You’ll tell them how you froze, how you thought your career was over, how you lay awake replaying it. And then you’ll tell them how you got through it. How you learned to be kinder to yourself. How you spoke again, and trembled, and still did it. And you’ll watch their shoulders drop, and their eyes soften, because they see that you survived. And then they’ll know they can, too.

I am allowed to move on. And I will.” Because you are, and you will. Not because you’re perfect, but because you’re learning. And that is enough. More than enough. It’s everything.

---

You might be familiar with the Buddhist concept of the **second arrow**. The first arrow is the pain itself—in your case, the freeze. The second arrow is the suffering we add on top of the pain: the shame, the rumination, the self-criticism, the “I can’t believe I did that,” the “what’s wrong with me?” The first arrow was unavoidable. The second arrow is optional, but we often shoot it at ourselves anyway. And we do it instantly, almost reflexively.

But the second arrow is still in flight—you’ve shot it into your own chest by replaying the moment, by telling yourself you’re mortified, by imagining what others thought. The first arrow hurt; the second arrow is keeping the wound open.

The good news is: you can put the second arrow down. You don’t have to keep throwing it at yourself. When the memory comes, that’s the first arrow—the pain of the memory. But when you add “I’m such an idiot,” that’s the second arrow. When you start imagining your reputation is ruined, that’s the second arrow. You can learn to notice the difference: *“This is the memory. This is the story I’m telling myself about it.”* The memory will pass. The story is what keeps you stuck.

So tonight, try this: let the first arrow be. Let the memory do its thing. But every time you catch yourself reaching for the second arrow—the shame, the self-blame—just notice it. Say, *“That’s the second arrow. I don’t have to pick that one up.”* And return to the present.

---

**Perfectionism often has deep roots.** For many people, the demand to be flawless in front of others isn’t just about the presentation. It’s an old survival strategy. Maybe when you were younger, you learned that being good, being smart, being the one who never made mistakes was the way to get approval, safety, or love. Mistakes felt dangerous—not because of the mistake itself, but because of what you feared the mistake would cost you: connection, status, belonging.

So when you froze, it wasn’t just a professional stumble. It may have triggered an old wound—the fear that if you are not perfect, you will be rejected. That’s why the mortification feels so outsized. Your brain isn’t just reacting to this one event. It’s reacting to years of accumulated pressure to be the one who gets it right. It’s reacting to the terrified child inside who learned that being less than perfect meant being less than loved.

If that resonates, then the work here is not just about public speaking. It’s about gently teaching that inner child: *You are safe. You are worthy even when you stumble. You don’t have to earn love through flawless performance.* That is deep, slow work. But every moment you choose self-compassion over self-criticism, you are sending that message. You are reparenting yourself.

---

**But what if there were real consequences?** Let’s not pretend that’s impossible. Maybe someone in the room did notice. Maybe your boss is wondering if you’re okay. Maybe there will be a follow-up conversation. That’s scary, but it’s also manageable. Here’s how to handle it with grace:

- **Be proactive, not reactive.** If this was a high-stakes presentation and you think it might affect someone’s perception of you, reach out to the key person within 24 hours. Keep it short and professional: “Yesterday was a bit rough for me—I lost my train of thought. I want to make sure the information I was trying to share gets through. Here is a summary of the key points I wanted to convey. Let me know if you have questions.” That’s all. No groveling, no over-explaining. You take responsibility for the outcome, you provide value, and you move on. This shows maturity and resilience, two things that matter more than one stumble.

- **If someone brings it up, own it lightly.** “Yeah, my brain decided to take a short vacation. Luckily, I have notes.” A little humor defuses tension and signals that you’re not shattered by it. If they offer sympathy, accept it with grace: “Thanks, I appreciate that. We got through it.” Don’t argue or defend. Just acknowledge and redirect.

- **Remember: one presentation rarely defines a person.** Unless this was a do-or-die moment—like a pitch to investors who have never met you and will never see you again—your reputation is built over time, not in 20 seconds. People will remember how you handle the aftermath more than the freeze itself. If you handle it with composure and follow-up, that will be the story. The freeze will fade into the background.

---

**Try this exercise.** Not tonight, maybe, but soon. Find a quiet moment and write a letter to yourself. Address it to the part of you that froze. Write it from the perspective of a wise, kind, older friend—someone who loves you unconditionally. What would they say? They might say: *“I saw you struggle today, and my heart went out to you. I know how much you wanted to do well. I know how hard you worked. And I want you to know that it’s okay. It’s okay to be nervous. It’s okay to lose your place. It’s okay to be human. I’m proud of you for getting through it. I’m proud of you for caring. And I’ll be here tomorrow, no matter what.”*

Write as much as you can. Let the kind voice speak. Then read it out loud. Let the words land. This is not fluffy self-help; this is practicing the voice you need to internalize. The more you practice it, the louder it gets, and the quieter the inner critic becomes.

---

**Humor as medicine.** I’m not saying you should laugh about this today. But one day, you might. Humor is one of the most powerful ways we reclaim power from shame. When you can tell the story of your freeze with a wry smile—“So I froze in front of 50 people, and my brain just left the building. It was epic”—you have taken the sting out. You have turned it into a story, and stories are safe. Stories are shareable. Stories connect us.

The fact that you can imagine telling it as a story means you have already begun to heal. The freeze is no longer a wound; it’s a tale from the road. And you, the storyteller, are still walking.

---

**Growth is not linear.** You might feel okay right now, and then at 2 a.m. the cringe will hit you again like a wave. That’s normal. The brain processes in cycles. Don’t panic if the feeling comes back. Just ride it. Say: *“Okay, this is the wave. It’s just a feeling. It will pass.”* Each time you ride a wave without fighting it, you teach your brain that the feeling is survivable. Over time, the waves get smaller and further apart. But it takes time. Be patient with yourself.

And when you do feel better—and you will—don’t be surprised if the lesson lingers. Not as shame, but as wisdom. You will know what it feels like to be the person in the audience who sees someone else freeze. And you will send them a silent wave of support: *I know, I’ve been there. You’re going to be okay.* That empathy is a gift born from your pain. It makes you more human, more connected, more real.

---

**Finally, let me say this as clearly as I can: You are not your freeze. You are not the story your inner critic is telling. You are not the sum of your worst moment. You are a person who showed up, who tried, who cared, and who is now brave enough to sit with the discomfort and learn from it. That is not failure. That is courage. That is resilience. That is growth. And that is something to be deeply proud of.**

So go gently. Put down the second arrow. Forgive yourself for being human. And trust that this, too, will become part of your story—not as a scar, but as a point of strength. You are allowed to move on. And you will.

One moment at a time. One breath at a time. You’re already doing it. Keep going.

analysis_pairs.text_N1:
And now we’re past the initial shock, past the immediate soothing, and we’re standing at the edge of something deeper: **the realization that this moment—this exact painful, cringing, awful moment—is actually a threshold.**

You can feel it, can’t you? Beneath the embarrassment, there’s a quiet stirring. A sense that this matters, that it’s asking something of you. Not that it’s a punishment or a sign to stop, but an invitation to change how you relate to yourself. And maybe you’re not ready to say yes to that invitation yet. Maybe you’re still too raw. That’s okay. The threshold doesn’t disappear. It waits.

But let’s sit with that idea for a moment. What if this freeze wasn’t just an accident? What if it was the end of one way of being and the beginning of another?

Many people go their whole lives without ever being cracked open like this. They stay safely inside their competence, never risking enough to freeze, never feeling the hot flush of exposure. And they also never taste the profound relief of discovering that they can survive their own imperfection. You’ve just been initiated into a deeper kind of humanity. Not by choice, but by circumstance. And that changes you.

**The terror you felt—and the shame you’re feeling now—is the friction of an old identity trying to hold on.** The identity that says, “I must be polished. I must be in control. I must not show weakness.” That identity is exhausted. It’s been running the show for too long, and today it finally hit a wall. The freeze was its collapse. And now you’re being asked to build a new identity—one that is allowed to be a work in progress.

What would that new identity look like?

It would look like someone who can laugh at their own tangles. Someone who can say, “I totally lost my train of thought,” without their voice shaking. Someone who walks into a room knowing they might be brilliant, or they might stumble, and neither outcome determines their worth. Someone who doesn’t need to be the best speaker in the room, because they’re too busy being the most present person in the room. That person is not a fantasy. That person is you, just a few reps from now, a few hard moments from now, a few self-compassionate choices from now.

**But to become that person, you have to let this version of you grieve.** Grieve the loss of the image you had—the one who never freezes, the one who never fails. That image is dying, and that’s okay. It was a heavy image to carry. You’re allowed to put it down. You’re allowed to be smaller, softer, more human. You might even find that being human is a relief.

**Now, let’s talk about the body again, because it’s still holding some of this.** Shame has a physical signature. It lives in the chest, the stomach, the throat. It can feel like heat, or weight, or a knot, or a sinking sensation. You can try to think your way out of it, but the body doesn’t respond to logic. It responds to sensation and rhythm.

So here’s a simple practice you can do right now, sitting wherever you are:

Place your hand on your chest, just over your heart. Feel the warmth of your palm. Close your eyes if you can. Take one slow breath in, and let it out with a little sound—a sigh, a hum, a long exhale. Do it again. And again. As you breathe, silently say: *I am here. I am safe. This will pass.* Don’t worry if you don’t believe it yet. The body doesn’t need belief. It needs repetition. It needs the signal. You are telling your nervous system: *The danger is over. We survived. We can rest now.*

Do this whenever the cringe hits. Not to push the feeling away, but to hold it in a larger container. The feeling is just a wave. You are the ocean. The wave rises, it crests, it falls. You remain.

**And what about tomorrow? Here’s what tomorrow might look like if you let it be a day of quiet rebuilding:**

Wake up. Before you check your phone, place your hand on your chest again. Take three slow breaths. Say: *“I am allowed to have a hard day. And I am allowed to have a new day.”*

Then, do one ordinary thing with full attention. Make coffee. Feel the warmth of the cup. Taste it. Let the simple act ground you. You are not a disembodied ball of shame. You are a person drinking coffee.

If the memory comes, let it come. Say: *“Hello again. I see you. I’m not going to fight you. But I’m also not going to let you ruin my coffee.”* Then return to the warmth of the cup.

At some point, tell someone you trust. Not for advice, just for witness. Say: *“I froze during my presentation yesterday. I’m still feeling embarrassed. I just needed to say it out loud.”* Let them witness your humanity. Receive their care. This is how shame dies—in the light of connection.

Then, do one small thing that makes you feel a sliver of competence. Send an email. Make a call. Organize a drawer. Finish a task. Anything that reminds you: *I am capable. I am not broken. I just had a hard moment.*

And in the evening, before bed, write down three things you did today that were kind, or brave, or just plain human. It could be as simple as: *I got out of bed. I asked for support. I breathed through a wave of cringe.* These are not small things. They are the building blocks of a new relationship with yourself.

**This will not be the last time you feel exposed.** Life will hand you more moments like this—moments where you stumble, where you’re seen in your imperfection, where you’d rather disappear. But each time, you’ll have a little more practice. Each time, you’ll remember that you survived the last one. Each time, the shame will have less power and the self-compassion will have more. That is the slow, unglamorous, beautiful work of becoming someone who can be fully human in front of others.

**So, and?** Here’s the “and”: The and is that you’re still standing. The and is that the sun will rise tomorrow. The and is that this moment, as big as it feels, is just one pixel in the vast mosaic of your life. The and is that you are not alone, not now, not ever. The and is that this conversation, this reaching out, is already a sign of health. You didn’t collapse into silence. You turned toward connection. That is the whole game. That is the whole work.

And the and is also this: You are more than this moment. You are more than your worst 20 seconds. You are a person who cares, who tries, who stumbles, and who gets back up. And that is the most beautiful, most human, most genuine thing you can be.

So take a breath. Feel the ground beneath you. You’re here. You survived. And you’re already becoming.

That is the slow, unglamorous, beautiful work of becoming someone who can be fully human in front of others.

**So, and?** Here’s the “and”: The and is that you’re still standing. The and is that the sun will rise tomorrow. The and is that this moment, as big as it feels, is just one pixel in the vast mosaic of your life. The and is that you are not alone, not now, not ever. The and is that this conversation, this reaching out, is already a sign of health. You didn’t collapse into silence. You turned toward connection. That is the whole game. That is the whole work.

And the and is also this: You are more than this moment. You are more than your worst 20 seconds. You are a person who cares, who tries, who stumbles, and who gets back up. And that is the most beautiful, most human, most genuine thing you can be.

So take a breath. Feel the ground beneath you. You’re here. You survived. And you’re already becoming.

I’m sorry — that waiting period is brutal. If you’re pretty sure the Friday invite is a layoff, the most important things are: **don’t sign anything on the spot**, ask for everything in writing, and get clarity on pay, benefits, and deadlines.

Below is how severance usually works in the US and what to do in the meeting.

---

## 1. Is severance legally required in the US?

Usually, **no**. Most US employment is “at-will,” meaning an employer can terminate employment without cause and, unless there’s an exception, without severance.

Common exceptions where severance may be required or more likely:

- **Employment contract**: If your offer letter, contract, or executive agreement promises severance.
- **Company policy/handbook/severance plan**: If the employer has a written policy or past practice that creates a severance obligation.
- **Union/collective bargaining agreement**.
- **WARN Act or state “mini-WARN” laws**: For certain larger employers doing mass layoffs or plant closings, they may owe 60 days’ notice or 60 days of pay/benefits.
- **Discrimination/retaliation concerns**: If the layoff seems targeted because of age, race, disability, pregnancy, medical leave, whistleblowing, etc., you may have legal leverage — talk to an employment lawyer before signing.

---

## 2. The usual deal: severance in exchange for a release

In many layoffs, the employer offers severance **in exchange for you signing a separation/release agreement**. That agreement usually says you waive certain legal claims, such as discrimination, wrongful termination, or other employment claims.

Typical things they ask you to agree to:

- Release of claims
- Confidentiality about the separation or severance amount
- Non-disparagement
- Sometimes non-solicitation or non-compete language
- Return of company property
- Cooperation with transition, sometimes limited

Typical things you should get in return:

- Severance pay
- Possibly continued health coverage or COBRA subsidy
- Possibly outplacement services
- Payout of accrued vacation/PTO if required by state law or company policy
- Possibly bonus, commission, or equity treatment
- Neutral or positive reference, if negotiated

**Do not feel pressured to sign immediately.** It is very normal to say:  
> “I need time to review this carefully.”

---

## 3. How much severance is typical?

There is no universal rule, but common patterns are:

- **1 to 2 weeks of pay per year of service**
- Sometimes a minimum floor, such as **4 weeks or 1 month**
- For salaried/professional roles, sometimes **1 to 3 months**
- For executives or senior roles, sometimes **3 to 12+ months**
- In mass layoffs, companies may offer standardized packages, often less negotiable

Examples:

| Tenure | Possible severance range |
|---|---|
| Under 2 years | 2 to 8 weeks |
| 2–5 years | 4 to 12 weeks |
| 5–10 years | 8 weeks to 3+ months |
| 10+ years | 3 to 6+ months, sometimes more |

But this varies enormously by company, role, industry, location, and whether it is a mass layoff.

---

## 4. Lump sum vs. salary continuation

Severance may be paid as:

### Lump sum
You get the full amount, usually after signing the release and after any revocation period expires.

### Salary continuation
They continue paying you over weeks or months, sometimes on normal payroll dates.

Important questions if it is salary continuation:

- Does it stop if I get a new job?
- Do benefits continue during the severance period?
- Is it contingent on signing each week or complying with certain conditions?
- Does it affect unemployment benefits in my state?

In some states, severance can affect unemployment eligibility. In others, it may not. This depends heavily on state law and how the severance is characterized.

---

## 5. Health insurance and COBRA

Ask specifically:

- When does health insurance end?
- Is COBRA offered?
- Will the company pay part or all of COBRA premiums?
- For how long?
- What about dental/vision?
- What about HSA/FSA funds?

Common outcomes:

- Coverage ends on your last day of employment.
- Coverage ends at the end of the month.
- Employer subsidizes COBRA for 1–6 months.
- You are responsible for full COBRA cost, which can be expensive.

COBRA generally gives you the right to continue employer health coverage for up to 18 months, but you usually pay the full premium plus a small administrative fee. Some severance packages include a COBRA subsidy.

---

## 6. Final paycheck, PTO, bonuses, commissions

Ask about:

### Final paycheck
State law controls timing. Some states require immediate payment on termination; others allow until the next regular payday.

### Accrued PTO/vacation
Some states require payout of accrued vacation/PTO. In other states, it depends on company policy. If the company policy says PTO is paid out, they generally should follow it.

### Bonus
Ask:

- Will I receive a prorated bonus?
- Is my bonus discretionary or formula-based?
- Does the severance agreement address bonus?
- If I was terminated near bonus payout date, is there any acceleration or proration?

### Commissions
If you are in sales, ask for a written accounting of commissions earned, pending, or in progress.

---

## 7. Equity, RSUs, stock options

If you have equity, this can be one of the most important parts.

Ask:

- What happens to unvested RSUs/options?
- Is there accelerated vesting?
- What is my exercise window for vested options?
- Can the exercise window be extended?
- What happens if I cannot afford to exercise?
- Are there tax consequences?
- Is there a repurchase right?

For stock options, many plans give you only **90 days after termination** to exercise vested options, though some companies allow longer. If you have significant equity, this may be worth negotiating or getting legal/financial advice on.

---

## 8. 401(k), retirement, and benefits

Ask:

- What happens to my 401(k)?
- Am I fully vested in employer contributions?
- Can I roll it over to an IRA or new employer plan?
- Do I have an outstanding 401(k) loan? If so, when is it due?
- What happens to life insurance, disability insurance, commuter benefits, tuition reimbursement, etc.?

A 401(k) loan can become due shortly after separation. If not repaid, it may be treated as a taxable distribution.

---

## 9. WARN Act and mass layoffs

If this is part of a larger layoff, the federal WARN Act may apply.

Very generally, WARN may require **60 days’ advance notice** or **60 days of pay/benefits** for covered employers in certain mass layoffs or plant closings.

Some states have stronger “mini-WARN” laws, including California, New York, New Jersey, Illinois, and others.

If your employer suddenly lays off a large group without notice, ask:

> “Is this layoff subject to WARN or state notice requirements? Will employees receive WARN pay or pay in lieu of notice?”

---

## 10. Age discrimination rules if you are 40 or older

If you are **40 or older**, federal law gives special protections when an employer asks you to release age discrimination claims.

For many group layoffs, the employer may need to provide:

- A list of job titles/ages of people selected and not selected in the decision group
- At least **45 days** to consider the release in certain group termination programs
- Or at least **21 days** in some individual situations
- A **7-day revocation period** after signing

If you are over 40 and they hand you a release with a short deadline, ask:

> “Does this release involve age discrimination claims under the OWBPA? How many days do I have to consider it?”

---

## 11. What to do in the Friday meeting

Try to stay calm, take notes, and avoid arguing or signing anything immediately.

You can say:

> “I understand. Can you please provide all separation and severance documents in writing? I’ll need time to review them carefully.”

Important questions to ask:

### About the layoff
- “Is my role being eliminated?”
- “Is this a layoff/reduction in force, or are you asking me to resign?”
- “What is my official termination date?”
- “Will my separation be coded as a layoff, not misconduct or voluntary resignation?”

That last point matters for unemployment.

### About severance
- “Is severance being offered?”
- “How much?”
- “Is it lump sum or salary continuation?”
- “When will it be paid?”
- “Is it negotiable?”
- “What do I need to sign to receive it?”
- “How long do I have to decide?”

### About benefits
- “When does health insurance end?”
- “Will COBRA be subsidized?”
- “What happens to my HSA/FSA?”
- “What happens to life/disability insurance?”

### About pay and PTO
- “When will I receive my final paycheck?”
- “Will accrued PTO/vacation be paid out?”
- “Will I receive any bonus, commission, or incentive pay?”

### About equity/retirement
- “What happens to my RSUs/options?”
- “What is my exercise window?”
- “What happens to my 401(k), including employer match?”

### About references
- “What is the company’s reference policy?”
- “Will you provide a neutral or positive reference?”
- “Can we agree on what will be said to future employers?”

---

## 12. Do not sign immediately if you can avoid it

If they present a severance agreement, you can say:

> “I appreciate the offer. I need time to review the agreement and may want to consult an advisor. Please send me the full agreement and all supporting documents.”

If they pressure you:

> “I want to handle this professionally, but I’m not comfortable signing today. What is the latest date I can sign?”

If they say it expires immediately, ask:

> “Can you confirm in writing that the deadline is today and the reason for the deadline?”

Most reputable employers will give at least some time. If they refuse, that is a red flag.

---

## 13. Can you negotiate?

Sometimes yes, sometimes no. In mass layoffs, packages are often standardized, but you can still ask.

Things people negotiate:

- More weeks/months of severance
- COBRA subsidy
- PTO payout if unclear
- Prorated bonus
- Commission payout
- Accelerated equity vesting
- Extended option exercise window
- Outplacement services
- Neutral or positive reference
- Agreement on job title or reason for departure
- Removal or narrowing of non-compete/non-solicit language
- Later official termination date to preserve benefits or vesting
- Payment of legal fees for reviewing the agreement, especially for executives

A professional way to ask:

> “Thank you for the initial package. Given my tenure, contributions, and the circumstances of the layoff, I’d like to discuss whether the severance can be improved. Specifically, I’m asking for [X].”

Be specific. Don’t make it emotional or threatening. Make it businesslike.

---

## 14. If they ask you to resign instead of being laid off

Be careful.

If they say, “We’d prefer you resign,” understand that voluntary resignation can hurt your ability to get unemployment benefits and may affect severance.

You can say:

> “I am not resigning voluntarily. If the company is eliminating my role, I’d like this to be documented as a layoff/reduction in force.”

If they want you to resign in exchange for severance, get the terms in writing first.

---

## 15. Unemployment benefits

If you are laid off, you should generally consider filing for unemployment promptly.

Key points:

- Layoff usually means you were separated through no fault of your own.
- Severance may or may not affect unemployment depending on your state.
- If the employer contests your unemployment, that can complicate things.
- Try to get documentation that your separation was due to layoff/reduction in force.

File as soon as you can after separation. Processing can take time.

---

## 16. Red flags where you should talk to a lawyer before signing

Consider consulting an employment lawyer if any of these apply:

- You believe the layoff is discriminatory based on age, race, sex, pregnancy, disability, religion, national origin, etc.
- You recently took medical leave, FMLA leave, disability accommodation, or workers’ comp.
- You recently reported harassment, discrimination, safety issues, wage theft, or illegal conduct.
- You are pregnant or recently returned from pregnancy/parental leave.
- You are close to vesting, retirement, or a bonus payout.
- You have a non-compete that could block future work.
- You are on a visa.
- You were singled out while others in similar roles were retained.
- The severance agreement is unusually broad or vague.
- They pressure you to sign immediately.
- You have equity or compensation issues that are significant.

Many employment lawyers offer consultations, and some will review a severance agreement for a flat fee.

---

## 17. Practical things to do before Friday

If you still have access and can do so lawfully and without violating company policy:

- Save personal contacts you are allowed to keep.
- Download personal files that are not confidential company property.
- Note your manager/colleagues’ LinkedIn profiles or contact info.
- Save copies of pay stubs, offer letter, bonus plans, equity grants, and performance reviews if accessible.
- Do not take confidential company documents, customer lists, trade secrets, or data you are not entitled to keep.
- Prepare a list of questions for the meeting.
- Have a notebook or document ready to take notes.
- Avoid sending emotional emails or Slack messages.

---

## 18. A simple script for the meeting

If you want something short to remember:

> “I understand. Please confirm in writing that this is a layoff/reduction in force. I would like the full severance agreement, benefits information, final pay details, and any equity/PTO/bonus information in writing. I need time to review before signing.”

If they ask you to sign:

> “I’m not signing today. I need time to review the agreement carefully.”

If they ask if you have questions:

> “Yes. What is the severance amount, payment timing, benefits end date, COBRA treatment, PTO payout, bonus/commission treatment, equity treatment, and reference policy?”

If they ask if you accept:

> “I need to review the written terms before making a decision.”

---

## 19. If you get the severance agreement, check these clauses carefully

Look for:

- Exact severance amount and payment schedule
- Whether signing is required to receive already-owed wages/PTO
- Release of claims scope
- Confidentiality and non-disparagement
- Non-compete/non-solicit restrictions
- Cooperation obligations
- Reference language
- Return of property
- Clawback or repayment provisions
- Whether you are waiving anything you should not waive
- Whether the agreement says you will not contest unemployment
- Whether it includes a mutual non-disparagement clause
- Whether the company’s promises are actually written down

If something was promised verbally, get it in writing.

---

## 20. Bottom line

In the US, severance is usually **not automatic**, but many employers offer it in exchange for a signed release. The package may include pay, COBRA subsidy, outplacement, and other benefits. The most important things for you right now are:

1. **Don’t sign anything immediately.**
2. Ask for the full separation/severance package in writing.
3. Ask whether this is a layoff/reduction in force.
4. Ask about final pay, PTO, health insurance, COBRA, bonus, equity, and 401(k).
5. Ask how long you have to review.
6. Consider negotiating.
7. If anything feels suspicious or high-stakes, talk to an employment lawyer before signing.

If you want, you can tell me your state, tenure, whether this is part of a larger layoff, and whether you have equity or a non-compete, and I can help you think through what questions are most important for your situation.

Here’s the deeper playbook — what to do **before, during, and after Friday**, including scripts, negotiation moves, and traps to avoid.

This is general US information, not legal advice. If your situation is high-stakes, talk to an employment lawyer in your state before signing.

---

# 1. The Friday game plan

## Before the meeting

Do these quietly today or tomorrow.

### A. Get your personal house in order

If you still have access and can do so without violating policy:

- Save personal contacts.
- Save personal documents that are yours, not company confidential info.
- Download pay stubs if available.
- Save your offer letter, compensation plan, bonus plan, equity grants, and performance reviews if accessible.
- Screenshot or export personal non-confidential notes you may need.
- Remove personal browser logins from the work laptop if practical.
- Do not forward confidential company documents, customer lists, source code, financials, internal strategy docs, etc.

The goal is: **protect yourself without giving them a reason to accuse you of misconduct.**

---

### B. Prepare a simple meeting kit

Have:

- Notebook and pen
- Laptop or phone for notes
- Calendar invite details
- A list of questions
- A glass of water
- A quiet place if remote

If remote:

- Make sure your camera/mic work.
- Avoid being in a public place.
- Have your phone charged.
- Consider having a backup way to take notes if your computer is locked.

---

### C. Decide your posture

Your best posture is usually:

> Calm, professional, non-combative, and non-committal.

You do not need to confess anything, argue, negotiate on the spot, or sign.

Your main objective is:

> Get information in writing and preserve your options.

---

# 2. What the meeting will likely look like

Layoff meetings usually follow one of these patterns.

## Pattern 1: Short and scripted

They say something like:

> “We’re eliminating your role effective [date]. You’ll receive separation paperwork. HR will walk you through next steps.”

This is common in mass layoffs.

Your job: listen, take notes, ask for documents, do not sign.

---

## Pattern 2: “We’d like you to resign”

They may say:

> “We think it would be better if you resigned.”

Be careful.

If you resign voluntarily, you may hurt:

- Unemployment eligibility
- Severance leverage
- Narrative for future employers
- Potential legal claims

Say:

> “I am not choosing to resign. If the company is ending my employment, I’d like it documented as a layoff or reduction in force.”

If they say resignation is “better for your record,” ask:

> “Can you put that in writing, including how the company will characterize my departure to future employers and for unemployment purposes?”

---

## Pattern 3: “We’re moving you to a PIP”

Sometimes a layoff is disguised as performance management.

If they say you are being placed on a performance improvement plan, ask:

- “Is my role being eliminated?”
- “Is this an alternative to layoff?”
- “What happens if I do not complete the PIP?”
- “Is severance available instead?”
- “Can I review the PIP terms in writing?”

Do not sign a PIP immediately if you suspect it is a pretext.

---

## Pattern 4: “You’re being separated for cause”

If they claim misconduct or performance issues, stay calm.

Say:

> “I disagree with that characterization. Please provide the written basis and the separation documents.”

Do not get pulled into a debate. If they are trying to deny severance or unemployment by calling it “cause,” you may need a lawyer.

---

# 3. The exact script to use

If you want a simple script, use this:

> “I understand. Please confirm in writing that my employment is ending due to a layoff/reduction in force. I would like all separation and severance documents in writing. I need time to review them before signing anything.”

If they ask:

### “Do you have any questions?”

Say:

> “Yes. What is the severance amount, payment timing, benefits end date, COBRA treatment, PTO payout, bonus/commission treatment, equity treatment, and reference policy?”

### “Can you sign today?”

Say:

> “No, I need time to review the agreement.”

### “This offer expires today.”

Say:

> “Please confirm in writing that the offer expires today and the reason for the deadline.”

### “We need an answer now.”

Say:

> “I want to handle this professionally, but I’m not able to make a decision without reviewing the written terms.”

### “Are you saying you won’t sign?”

Say:

> “I’m saying I need time to review before deciding.”

### “Do you accept the separation?”

Say:

> “I need to review the written terms before making any decision.”

---

# 4. The key questions to ask

Bring this list.

## About the termination

- “Is this a layoff or reduction in force?”
- “Is my role being eliminated?”
- “What is my official last day?”
- “Will I remain employed through a notice period?”
- “Am I expected to work through the notice period or am I being paid in lieu?”
- “How will my departure be characterized internally and externally?”
- “Will you confirm I was laid off, not terminated for cause?”

---

## About severance

- “Is severance being offered?”
- “How much?”
- “How is it calculated?”
- “Is it lump sum or installments?”
- “When will it be paid?”
- “Is it contingent on signing a release?”
- “How long do I have to review the release?”
- “Is the severance negotiable?”
- “What happens if I do not sign?”
- “What happens to already-earned wages, PTO, bonuses, commissions, or expense reimbursements?”

Important: **They should not condition already-earned wages on signing a release.** They can condition extra severance on a release, but not your earned pay.

---

## About health insurance

- “When does health insurance end?”
- “Does coverage end on my last day or at the end of the month?”
- “Will COBRA be offered?”
- “Will the company subsidize COBRA?”
- “For how long?”
- “What about dental and vision?”
- “What happens to my HSA/FSA?”
- “Can I change benefits elections due to this qualifying life event?”

---

## About PTO and final pay

- “When will I receive my final paycheck?”
- “Will accrued PTO/vacation be paid out?”
- “How is PTO calculated?”
- “Will sick time be paid out?”
- “Are there any deductions?”
- “Will expense reimbursements be processed?”

Note: sick time often does not have to be paid out, but vacation/PTO may depending on state law and policy.

---

## About bonus/commission

- “Will I receive a prorated bonus?”
- “Is the bonus discretionary or formulaic?”
- “What is the bonus plan’s treatment of employees terminated before payout?”
- “If I earned a bonus but payout is after separation, will it be paid?”
- “For commissions, what is the commission plan’s treatment of pending deals?”
- “Can I get a written accounting of commissions?”

---

## About equity

If you have RSUs, options, or other equity:

- “What happens to unvested equity?”
- “Is there accelerated vesting?”
- “What happens to vested options?”
- “What is my exercise window?”
- “Can the exercise window be extended?”
- “What is the current fair market value?”
- “Are there tax withholding issues?”
- “Is there a repurchase right?”
- “Can I do a cashless exercise?”
- “What happens if I cannot afford to exercise?”

---

## About retirement and loans

- “Am I vested in my 401(k) employer match?”
- “What are my rollover options?”
- “Do I have a 401(k) loan?”
- “If so, when is it due?”

- Laptop or phone for notes

## Sample negotiation email

Subject: Severance Review — [Your Name]

> Thank you for the separation information. I have reviewed the initial terms and would like to discuss a few adjustments before signing.
>
> Given my tenure, role, and contributions, and the fact that this separation is due to a layoff/reduction in force, I am requesting:
>
> 1. Severance increased to [X weeks/months] of base pay.  
> 2. Company-paid COBRA or a COBRA stipend for [X months].  
> 3. Payout of accrued PTO/vacation in accordance with company policy/applicable law.  
> 4. Prorated bonus/commission for [year/quarter], if applicable.  
> 5. [Acceleration/extension] of equity vesting or extension of the option exercise window.  
> 6. A neutral or positive written reference confirming my role, dates of employment, and that my departure was part of a reduction in force.  
>
> I appreciate the support during this transition and am open to discussing a reasonable resolution. Please let me know when we can speak or whether you can provide a revised agreement.

Keep it calm, factual, and professional.

---

# 11. If they agree to negotiate

Get every change in writing.

Do not rely on verbal assurances like:

- “Don’t worry about that clause.”
- “We won’t enforce that.”
- “HR said it’s fine.”
- “You’ll still get the bonus later.”
- “We’ll extend your insurance, but it’s not in the agreement yet.”

If it matters, it needs to be in the signed document or an amendment.

You can say:

> “Thanks. Please send a revised agreement reflecting those changes so I can review the final version.”

---

# 12. If they say no

If they say the package is final, you still have choices.

You can ask:

> “Can you confirm that this is the final offer and that no exceptions will be made?”

Then decide whether to:

- Sign as-is
- Ask for one or two specific improvements
- Consult a lawyer before signing
- Decline to sign and preserve your options

If you decline to sign, understand the tradeoff:

- You may lose the severance offer
- You may preserve legal claims
- You may still be entitled to earned wages, PTO where required, benefits continuation info, COBRA rights, unemployment, etc.

If the agreement includes questionable clauses or you suspect discrimination/retaliation, talk to a lawyer before rejecting it.

---

# 13. Signing logistics

If you decide to sign, pay attention to the mechanics.

## Check:

- Are all negotiated terms included?
- Is the payment amount correct?
- Is the payment date clear?
- Is the separation date correct?
- Is the reason for separation stated correctly, if stated at all?
- Are benefits end dates correct?
- Are equity terms accurate?
- Are there any blanks or missing exhibits?
- Is the company signatory authorized?
- Do you get a fully executed copy?

## Ask for:

- A fully signed copy
- A copy of the original plan documents if referenced
- A final pay statement
- COBRA election materials
- Benefits termination information
- Equity status statement
- Reference letter, if agreed
- Separation certificate or layoff confirmation, if possible

---

# 14. If there is a revocation period

Some agreements, especially those involving age discrimination claims for employees 40 or older, include a revocation period.

For example, you may have 7 days after signing to revoke.

If you sign and later realize something is wrong, act quickly.

To revoke, usually you must provide written notice within the revocation period. Follow the agreement’s instructions exactly.

If you revoke, you generally lose the severance but preserve your claims.

---

Once the meeting is over, do this:

## A. Write down everything while fresh

Record:

- Date/time of meeting
- Who was present
- What they said
- Whether they said “layoff,” “reduction in force,” “separation,” “resignation,” or “termination”
- Any deadlines
- Any promises
- Any pressure to sign
- Any mention of performance, conduct, WARN, severance, benefits, equity, etc.

Do this from memory as soon as possible.

---

## B. Organize documents

Create a folder for:

- Meeting notes
- Severance agreement
- Benefits documents
- Pay stubs
- Offer letter
- Equity documents
- Bonus/commission plan
- Employee handbook
- Emails from HR
- COBRA paperwork
- Final paycheck details
- Unemployment confirmation
- Reference agreement

---

Make a deadline list:

- Deadline to sign severance
- Deadline to revoke
- COBRA election deadline
- Option exercise deadline
- 401(k) loan repayment deadline

Ask:

- “Will taxes be withheld?”
- “At what rate?”
- “Can I adjust withholding?”
- “Will I receive a W-2 for the severance?”

If the amount is large, consider consulting a tax professional, especially if you have equity income, bonuses, or other complications.

---

# 40. Severance and unemployment, by state

This varies a lot.

General patterns:

| State approach | Effect |
|---|---|
| Severance does not affect unemployment | You can file immediately and receive benefits, severance is separate |
| Severance delays or reduces benefits | Benefits may be offset week-by-week |
| Lump sum treated differently from salary continuation | One may affect benefits, the other may not |
| Depends on whether severance is tied to a release | Some states treat it differently |

Examples (general, not legal advice):

- **California**: Severance usually does not disqualify you from unemployment.
- **New York**: Severance may reduce benefits if paid as wages or salary continuation.
- **Texas**: Severance may affect benefits depending on how it is paid.
- **Florida**: Severance can affect eligibility in some cases.

Check your state unemployment agency website or call them. If unsure, file anyway and let them determine eligibility.

---

# 41. If you get a new job quickly

If you find a new job before the severance period ends:

- Check whether severance stops or continues.
- Some agreements say severance ends if you get new employment.
- Some say it continues regardless.
- Salary continuation is more likely to stop; lump sums are less likely to be clawed back.

Ask:

> “If I obtain new employment during the severance period, does severance continue or stop?”

If it stops, ask whether you can receive the remaining balance as a lump sum.

Also check:

- Do benefits continue?
- Does COBRA subsidy continue?
- Does the non-compete or non-solicit kick in?

---

# 42. The emotional side

Layoffs are stressful. It is normal to feel:

- Shock
- Anger
- Embarrassment
- Fear
- Relief, sometimes

Try to:

- Avoid making big decisions the same day.
- Talk to someone you trust.
- Sleep and eat normally if possible.
- Do not send emotional emails or social media posts.
- Give yourself a few days before deciding anything major.

You do not have to “be fine” immediately. But protect your professional interests while you process.

---

# 43. Job search practicalities

Once the dust settles:

## Update your materials

- Resume
- LinkedIn profile
- Portfolio, if relevant
- List of accomplishments with metrics

## Network

- Let trusted people know you are open.
- Reach out to former colleagues.
- Contact recruiters.
- Ask for introductions.

## LinkedIn

You can choose whether to announce your layoff. Many people do, and it can generate support. But wait until you understand any confidentiality or non-disparagement terms.

A simple post:

> “After [X years] at [Company], my role was affected by a reduction in force. I’m now open to opportunities in [field]. If you know of roles or teams hiring, I’d appreciate a message.”

Keep it positive and forward-looking.

---

# 44. When to hire an employment lawyer

Consider a lawyer if:

- You suspect discrimination or retaliation.
- You are over 40 and the timeline feels rushed.
- You have a non-compete that could block work.
- You are on a visa.
- You have significant equity or deferred compensation.
- The agreement is confusing or one-sided.
- They pressure you to sign immediately.
- They claim “cause” or deny earned pay.
- You are close to vesting, retirement, or bonus payout.
- You were singled out while similar employees were retained.
- You recently took protected leave or requested accommodation.

Many lawyers offer:

- Free or low-cost consultations
- Flat-fee agreement reviews
- Hourly advice
- Negotiation assistance

You do not need to sue to benefit from a lawyer. Sometimes a one-hour review is enough.

---

# 45. Final checklist

## Before Friday

- [ ] Save personal contacts and allowed documents.
- [ ] Gather pay stubs, offer letter, equity docs, bonus plans.
- [ ] Prepare a notebook and question list.
- [ ] Decide your main goal: get info in writing, do not sign.

- [ ] Ask if this is a layoff/reduction in force.
- [ ] Ask for all documents in writing.
- [ ] Do not sign anything.
- [ ] Ask about severance, benefits, PTO, bonus, equity, reference.
- [ ] Ask how long you have to review.

- [ ] Write down everything.
- [ ] Organize documents.
- [ ] Review the agreement carefully.
- [ ] Check deadlines.
- [ ] Consider negotiating.
- [ ] File for unemployment if applicable.
- [ ] Consult a lawyer if needed.
- [ ] Take care of yourself.

---

## The core message

You do not have to decide anything in the moment.

Your safest move is:

> “I need time to review the agreement before signing anything.”

Get everything in writing. Protect your earned compensation. Preserve your options. Then decide calmly.

And here’s the **“don’t mess this up” layer** — the stuff people forget in the moment.

---

## 1. If they send a DocuSign during the meeting

Do **not** sign just because it appears on screen.

Say:

> “Please send it to my personal email so I can review it carefully.”

If they say you must sign now:

> “I’m not able to sign without time to review. Please confirm the deadline in writing.”

Signing an electronic release is still signing.

---

## 2. If they ask you to sign an “acknowledgment”

There’s a difference between:

- **Acknowledgment of receipt**: “I received these documents.”
- **Release/agreement**: “I waive claims and accept severance terms.”

If they ask you to sign anything, ask:

> “Is this only an acknowledgment that I received documents, or is it a release/agreement?”

If it is a release, do not sign immediately.

If you are unsure, say:

> “I’m not signing anything until I’ve had time to review it.”

---

## 3. If they ask, “Do you have any claims against the company?”

Do not answer substantively.

Say:

> “I’m not prepared to answer that right now. I need to review the separation documents first.”

Do not say:

- “No, I have no claims.”
- “I won’t sue.”
- “Everything was fair.”
- “I understand why this happened.”

You do not need to help them build their protection.

---

## 4. If they ask, “Do you accept the separation?”

Careful. You can acknowledge the meeting without accepting a characterization.

Say:

> “I understand the company is ending my employment. I need the terms in writing.”

Avoid saying:

> “I accept.”
> “I agree.”
> “I resign.”
> “This is mutual.”

If this is a layoff, you want it described as a layoff/reduction in force.

---

## 5. If they say, “We’d prefer to call it a mutual separation”

Ask what that means in writing.

Say:

> “If it is a mutual separation, please provide the written terms, including severance, reference language, and how my departure will be described.”

A “mutual separation” can sometimes hurt unemployment or weaken your position. Do not agree to that label unless the written deal is good.

---

## 6. If they ask you to return your laptop before you save personal info

Ask for time.

Say:

> “I need a reasonable opportunity to remove personal files and log out of personal accounts before returning company equipment.”

If they demand immediate return:

> “Please provide written instructions and a receipt when I return the equipment.”

Before returning:

- Log out of personal accounts.
- Remove personal photos/files if allowed.
- Do not delete work files unless instructed.
- Do not take confidential company data.

---

## 7. If they say, “You can access your personal files after”

Do not rely on that.

Once access is cut, it may be gone.

If possible, before the meeting or immediately after:

- Save personal contacts.
- Save personal documents.
- Save pay statements.
- Save offer letter, bonus plan, equity docs, reviews.
- Save anything that proves your compensation or performance.

But again: **no confidential company documents, customer data, source code, trade secrets, etc.**

---

## 8. If they ask you to stay for a transition period

Ask whether you will be paid and what the terms are.

Say:

> “I’m open to a reasonable transition, but I need the terms in writing, including pay, duties, duration, and benefits.”

Important questions:

- Am I still employed during the transition?
- Am I paid my normal salary?
- Do benefits continue?
- How many hours are expected?
- Can I interview for other jobs during that time?
- Does this affect severance?
- Does this affect unemployment?

Do not let them get free transition help while calling it “severance.”

---

## 9. If they offer “garden leave” or paid notice

Ask:

- “Am I still employed during the notice period?”
- “Do benefits continue?”
- “Does equity continue vesting?”
- “Can I use PTO?”
- “When is my official separation date?”
- “Can I start a new job during the notice period?”
- “Is this notice pay separate from severance?”

The difference matters for health insurance, vesting, 401(k), unemployment, and immigration.

---

## 10. If they ask you to certify you have returned all company property

Only certify if it is true.

Say:

> “I can confirm return once we have a written list and I receive a receipt.”

If you still have something, say:

> “I still have [item]. Please tell me the return process.”

Do not falsely certify. That can become a problem later.

---

## 11. If they ask you to delete social media or personal posts

You do not have to agree on the spot.

Say:

> “I need to review that request in writing.”

If they are asking you to remove posts about workplace issues, that may raise legal concerns. Talk to a lawyer before agreeing.

---

## 12. If they ask you not to talk to coworkers

Be careful.

In some situations, employees have protected rights to discuss wages, working conditions, layoffs, and legal rights.

Say:

> “Please put that instruction in writing.”

Do not agree to broad silence unless you understand the scope.

---

## 13. If they ask you to participate in an internal investigation

If you suspect discrimination, retaliation, or wrongdoing, be cautious.

Say:

> “I need time to consider. Please send the request in writing.”

You may want to speak to a lawyer before giving a formal statement.

---

## 14. If they ask whether you intend to sue

Do not answer.

Say:

> “I’m not prepared to discuss that. I need to review the separation agreement.”

Or:

> “I’m focused on understanding the separation terms right now.”

Do not threaten litigation in the meeting unless you are ready for that path.

---

## 15. If they ask whether you have another job

You do not need to answer.

Say:

> “I’m not prepared to discuss that.”

Or:

> “I’m focused on the separation terms right now.”

Your job search is not their business unless it affects a specific written term.

---

## 16. If they say, “This is standard”

“Standard” does not mean you cannot ask questions or negotiate.

Say:

> “I understand it may be standard, but I still need to review it and may have questions.”

Or:

> “Even if it is standard, I need time before signing.”

---

## 17. If they say, “Everyone is getting the same package”

That may be true, but still ask:

- “What is the formula?”
- “Is it based on tenure, level, or role?”
- “Are there exceptions?”
- “Can I request adjustments based on my circumstances?”

Even standardized packages can sometimes be adjusted for equity, bonus, benefits, reference language, or transition terms.

---

## 18. If they say, “If you don’t sign, you get nothing”

Ask for clarification.

Say:

> “Please confirm in writing what I will receive if I do not sign, including final wages, accrued PTO, expense reimbursements, earned bonus/commissions, and benefits information.”

They can condition **extra severance** on a release, but they generally cannot withhold already-earned wages or benefits required by law.

---

## 19. If they say, “You can’t get unemployment if you sign”

That is suspicious.

Say:

> “Please put that in writing.”

In many places, you cannot waive unemployment rights, and a layoff should generally allow you to file. If they try to block unemployment, talk to a lawyer or your state unemployment agency.

---

## 20. If they say, “You can’t talk about your severance”

Ask what exactly is confidential.

Say:

> “Please clarify the confidentiality provision in writing.”

Some confidentiality clauses are limited by law. Do not assume you can discuss it freely, but also do not assume you cannot discuss it without reading the agreement.

---

## 21. If they say, “You can’t work for competitors”

Ask:

> “Please point me to the specific non-compete provision and explain the scope, duration, and geographic limits.”

If the severance agreement adds a new non-compete, ask:

> “What additional consideration is being provided for this restriction?”

If your ability to get another job is affected, this may be worth legal review.

---

## 22. If they say, “You need to sign to get your final paycheck”

That is a major red flag.

Say:

> “Please confirm in writing that my final paycheck and earned wages are being conditioned on signing the release.”

In many states, final wages are owed regardless of whether you sign a severance release.

---

## 23. If they say, “You need to sign to get your PTO payout”

Also a red flag.

Say:

> “Please clarify whether accrued PTO payout is required by company policy or state law, and whether it is being conditioned on signing the release.”

In some states, accrued vacation/PTO must be paid out. In others, it depends on policy. But earned compensation should not be held hostage.

---

## 24. If they say, “You need to sign to get COBRA”

COBRA rights are generally legal rights, not a favor.

Say:

> “Please provide the COBRA election materials and confirm my rights in writing.”

If they condition COBRA on signing a release, that needs careful review.

---

## 25. If they say, “You’re not eligible for rehire”

Ask:

> “Please confirm that in writing.”

This can affect references and future opportunities. If the reason is inaccurate, you may want to negotiate correction.

---

## 26. If they say, “We’ll give you a positive reference”

Say:

> “Please put that in writing.”

Ask for:

- Who will give the reference
- What they will say
- Whether they will confirm layoff/reduction in force
- Whether they will say you are eligible for rehire
- Whether they will provide a written letter

---

## 27. If they say, “We’ll announce that you left voluntarily”

Be careful.

Ask:

> “Can we agree in writing that my departure will be described as a layoff/reduction in force?”

If they insist on saying you left voluntarily, understand how that may affect unemployment, references, and your narrative.

---

## 28. If they say, “You can keep your laptop”

Get it in writing.

Say:

> “Please confirm in writing that I am permitted to retain the laptop and that it has been transferred to me or that I may purchase it for $0/$1.”

Otherwise they could later demand it back or claim it was not returned.

---

## 29. If they say, “You can keep your phone number”

Ask:

> “Please confirm the process for transferring my phone number and that I will not be charged.”

If it is a company phone, you may need to port the number out before access ends.

---

## 30. If they say, “You can keep your email address”

Ask:

> “Please confirm in writing whether I can retain or forward my work email, and for how long.”

Do not assume you will have access later.

---

## 31. If they say, “You can access your files later”

Ask:

> “Please confirm in writing what files, for how long, and how I will access them.”

If possible, get your personal files before the meeting ends.

---

## 32. If they say, “We’ll pay you through [date]”

Ask:

> “Am I employed through that date, or is that pay in lieu of notice?”

This matters for:

- Health insurance
- Equity vesting
- 401(k) match
- PTO accrual
- Unemployment
- Immigration status

---

## 33. If they say, “Your last day is today”

Ask:

> “Will I be paid through today? When is my final paycheck? Do benefits end today or at month-end?”

Also ask:

- “Will I receive pay in lieu of notice?”
- “Will I receive WARN pay if applicable?”
- “How will my separation be coded?”
- “When do I need to return equipment?”
- “How will I receive COBRA materials?”

---

## 34. If they say, “Your last day is next month”

Ask:

- “Am I expected to work?”
- “Am I on paid notice?”
- “Do benefits continue?”
- “Do I continue vesting?”
- “Can I interview?”
- “Can I start a new job early?”
- “Can I use PTO?”
- “What happens if I find a job before then?”

---

## 35. If they say, “You’re being laid off, but we want you to apply for other roles”

Ask:

- “Am I guaranteed consideration?”
- “Is my current role actually eliminated?”
- “Will I be interviewed?”
- “Will severance be affected if I apply or don’t apply?”
- “Can I decline without losing severance?”

Internal transfer can be good, but do not let it blur the fact that your current role is ending.

---

## 36. If they say, “You can transfer to another team”

Ask:

- “Is the new role guaranteed?”
- “What is the compensation?”
- “What is the start date?”
- “Do I keep tenure and benefits?”
- “What happens if the new role does not work out?”
- “Can I still take severance instead?”

Get it in writing.

---

## 37. If they say, “You’re being reassigned”

Ask:

- “Is this a termination of my current role?”
- “Is my compensation changing?”
- “Is my title changing?”
- “Is my location changing?”
- “Do I have the right to decline?”
- “If I decline, is that considered resignation?”

If the reassignment is a significant downgrade, it may affect your rights.

- “Am I still employed?”

- “Is there a return date?”

- Severance
